subject: math
title: Grade 6 Volume and Capacity
seo_title: Grade 6 Volume and Capacity Worksheets: Free Math Practice with Answer Key (BC Curriculum)
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 math worksheets on volume and capacity for the BC curriculum: counting cubes, V = l × w × h, millilitres and litres, 1 cm³ = 1 mL, and word problems about fish tanks, boxes and water tanks. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Volume of a box = length × width × height. 1 cm³ holds 1 mL, and 1000 mL = 1 L.
key_sub: Multiply the three edges (do not add them) and write cubic units: cm³, m³. To change cm³ to litres, divide by 1000.
body_html:
What volume means

Volume is the amount of space a solid takes up. A cube with 1 cm edges has a volume of 1 cm³ (one cubic centimetre). To find a volume, count how many of these cubes fill the solid.

The formula: V = l × w × h

Length × width tells you how many cubes are in one layer. The height tells you how many layers there are. So V = l × w × h, and the answer is in cubic units (cm³, m³).

Example 1

A box is 8 cm long, 5 cm wide and 3 cm high. What is its volume?

V = 8 × 5 × 3 = 40 × 3.

Answer: 120 cm³

Capacity: millilitres and litres

Capacity is how much a container can hold. We measure it in millilitres (mL) and litres (L). 1 L = 1000 mL, so multiply by 1000 to change litres to millilitres, and divide by 1000 to go back.

Volume and capacity together

A 1 cm³ container holds exactly 1 mL. A cube with 10 cm edges has a volume of 1000 cm³, so it holds 1000 mL, which is 1 L.

VolumeCapacity
1 cm³1 mL
1000 cm³ (a 10 cm cube)1 L
1 m³1000 L
Example 2

A fish tank is 60 cm long, 30 cm wide and 40 cm high. How many litres does it hold?

V = 60 × 30 × 40 = 72 000 cm³ = 72 000 mL. Divide by 1000.

Answer: 72 L

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Adding the edges: 6 + 4 + 5 = 15Multiply them: 6 × 4 × 5 = 120
Stopping at one layer: 6 × 4 = 24Multiply by the height too
Counting only the cubes you can seeCount every layer, hidden cubes too
Writing cm² for a volumeVolume is in cubic units: cm³, m³
2.5 L = 2005 mL2.5 × 1000 = 2500 mL
Multiplying by 100 for mL1 L = 1000 mL, so use 1000

faq.q: How do you find the volume of a rectangular prism in Grade 6?
faq.a: Multiply length × width × height. A box 6 cm long, 4 cm wide and 5 cm high has a volume of 6 × 4 × 5 = 120 cm³.

faq.q: What is the difference between volume and capacity?
faq.a: Volume is the space a solid takes up, in cubic units like cm³. Capacity is how much a container holds, in mL or L.

faq.q: How many millilitres are in 1 cubic centimetre?
faq.a: Exactly 1 mL. So 1000 cm³ = 1000 mL = 1 L, and a box with a volume of 72 000 cm³ holds 72 L.

faq.q: Is volume part of the BC Grade 6 math curriculum?
faq.a: Yes. The BC Grade 6 Geometry and measurement standards include volume and capacity: finding the volume of rectangular prisms and connecting cm³ to mL and L.

items.q: A cube has edges that are 1 cm long. What is its volume?
items.e: A cube with 1 cm edges is the unit for volume: 1 cm³ (one cubic centimetre). 1 cm² is the area of one face, and 1 cm is the length of one edge.

items.q: Each small cube is 1 cm³. What is the volume of this prism?
items.e: The bottom layer has 2 rows of 5 cubes = 10 cubes. There are 2 layers: 10 × 2 = 20 cm³. Count the hidden cubes too: only 16 cubes show a face.

items.q: Each small cube is 1 cm³. What is the volume of this prism?
items.e: The bottom layer has 3 rows of 3 cubes = 9 cubes. There are 2 layers: 9 × 2 = 18 cm³. Count the hidden cubes too: only 14 cubes show a face.

items.q: Each small cube is 1 cm³. What is the volume of this prism?
items.e: The bottom layer has 3 rows of 3 cubes = 9 cubes. There are 4 layers: 9 × 4 = 36 cm³. Count the hidden cubes too: only 24 cubes show a face.

items.q: Each small cube is 1 cm³. What is the volume of this prism?
items.e: The bottom layer has 2 rows of 2 cubes = 4 cubes. There are 2 layers: 4 × 2 = 8 cm³. Count the hidden cubes too: only 7 cubes show a face.

items.q: Each small cube is 1 cm³. What is the volume of this prism?
items.e: The bottom layer has 3 rows of 4 cubes = 12 cubes. There are 4 layers: 12 × 4 = 48 cm³. Count the hidden cubes too: only 30 cubes show a face.

items.q: Each small cube is 1 cm³. What is the volume of this prism?
items.e: The bottom layer has 3 rows of 5 cubes = 15 cubes. There are 2 layers: 15 × 2 = 30 cm³. Count the hidden cubes too: only 22 cubes show a face.

items.q: Each small cube is 1 cm³. What is the volume of this prism?
items.e: The bottom layer has 3 rows of 4 cubes = 12 cubes. There are 3 layers: 12 × 3 = 36 cm³. Count the hidden cubes too: only 24 cubes show a face.

items.q: How many centimetre cubes are in the bottom layer of this prism?
items.e: The bottom layer is 5 cubes long and 4 cubes deep: 5 × 4 = 20 cubes. The front face shows 5 × 3 = 15 cubes, but that is not a layer.

items.q: How many centimetre cubes are in the bottom layer of this prism?
items.e: The bottom layer is 4 cubes long and 2 cubes deep: 4 × 2 = 8 cubes. The front face shows 4 × 4 = 16 cubes, but that is not a layer.

items.q: How many centimetre cubes are in the bottom layer of this prism?
items.e: The bottom layer is 3 cubes long and 2 cubes deep: 3 × 2 = 6 cubes. The front face shows 3 × 4 = 12 cubes, but that is not a layer.

items.q: How many centimetre cubes are in the bottom layer of this prism?
items.e: The bottom layer is 4 cubes long and 3 cubes deep: 4 × 3 = 12 cubes. The front face shows 4 × 2 = 8 cubes, but that is not a layer.

items.q: The layers of this prism are pulled apart. Each cube is 1 cm³. What is the volume of the whole prism?
items.e: One layer: 4 × 2 = 8 cubes. 2 layers: 8 × 2 = 16 cm³.

items.q: The layers of this prism are pulled apart. Each cube is 1 cm³. What is the volume of the whole prism?
items.e: One layer: 5 × 3 = 15 cubes. 4 layers: 15 × 4 = 60 cm³.

items.q: The layers of this prism are pulled apart. Each cube is 1 cm³. What is the volume of the whole prism?
items.e: One layer: 3 × 2 = 6 cubes. 3 layers: 6 × 3 = 18 cm³.

items.q: The layers of this prism are pulled apart. Each cube is 1 cm³. What is the volume of the whole prism?
items.e: One layer: 4 × 2 = 8 cubes. 3 layers: 8 × 3 = 24 cm³.

items.q: The bottom layer of a box holds 6 rows of 4 centimetre cubes. The box holds 5 layers. What is the volume of the box?
items.e: One layer: 6 × 4 = 24 cubes. 5 layers: 24 × 5 = 120 cm³.

items.q: The bottom layer of a tray holds 8 rows of 5 centimetre cubes. The tray holds 3 layers. What is the volume of the tray?
items.e: One layer: 8 × 5 = 40 cubes. 3 layers: 40 × 3 = 120 cm³.

items.q: How many 1 cm cubes fit in a box that is 10 cm long, 6 cm wide and 4 cm high?
items.e: Bottom layer: 10 × 6 = 60 cubes. The box is 4 cm high, so it holds 4 layers: 60 × 4 = 240 cubes. (20 adds the edges, 60 is only one layer, and 64 adds the height to one layer.)

items.q: A box holds 60 centimetre cubes in each layer. It holds 420 cubes in all. How many layers are there?
items.e: Cubes in one layer × number of layers = total, so 60 × ? = 420. 420 ÷ 60 = 7 layers. (360 subtracts and 480 adds.)

sets.title: Rectangular prisms: V = l × w × h

items.q: What is the volume of this rectangular prism?
items.e: V = l × w × h = 13 × 3 × 12 = 39 × 12 = 468 cm³. Multiply all three edges (do not add them), and write cubic units.

items.q: What is the volume of this rectangular prism?
items.e: V = l × w × h = 10 × 9 × 4 = 90 × 4 = 360 cm³. Multiply all three edges (do not add them), and write cubic units.

items.q: What is the volume of this rectangular prism?
items.e: V = l × w × h = 9 × 2 × 4 = 18 × 4 = 72 cm³. Multiply all three edges (do not add them), and write cubic units.

items.q: What is the volume of this rectangular prism?
items.e: V = l × w × h = 8 × 4 × 5 = 32 × 5 = 160 m³. Multiply all three edges (do not add them), and write cubic units.

items.q: What is the volume of this rectangular prism?
items.e: V = l × w × h = 8 × 5 × 7 = 40 × 7 = 280 cm³. Multiply all three edges (do not add them), and write cubic units.

items.q: What is the volume of this rectangular prism?
items.e: V = l × w × h = 12 × 7 × 5 = 84 × 5 = 420 cm³. Multiply all three edges (do not add them), and write cubic units.

items.q: What is the volume of this rectangular prism?
items.e: V = l × w × h = 4 × 2 × 2 = 8 × 2 = 16 m³. Multiply all three edges (do not add them), and write cubic units.

items.q: What is the volume of this rectangular prism?
items.e: V = l × w × h = 12 × 6 × 9 = 72 × 9 = 648 cm³. Multiply all three edges (do not add them), and write cubic units.

items.q: A cube has edges that are 5 cm long. What is its volume?
items.e: All the edges of a cube are equal, so V = 5 × 5 × 5 = 25 × 5 = 125 cm³. 5 × 3 = 15 is not the volume.

items.q: A cube has edges that are 8 cm long. What is its volume?
items.e: All the edges of a cube are equal, so V = 8 × 8 × 8 = 64 × 8 = 512 cm³. 8 × 3 = 24 is not the volume.

items.q: A cube has edges that are 10 cm long. What is its volume?
items.e: All the edges of a cube are equal, so V = 10 × 10 × 10 = 100 × 10 = 1000 cm³. 10 × 3 = 30 is not the volume.

items.q: A box is 6 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high. Which expression gives its volume?
items.e: Volume = length × width × height = 6 × 4 × 3 = 72 cm³. 6 × 4 is only the area of the base.

items.q: A recycling bin is 50 cm long, 30 cm wide and 20 cm high. Which expression gives its volume?
items.e: Length × width × height = 50 × 30 × 20 = 1500 × 20 = 30 000 cm³. (50 + 30) × 20 adds two edges first.

items.q: What is the volume of this rectangular prism?
items.e: V = 2.5 × 4 × 6 = 10 × 6 = 60 cm³. Multiply decimals the same way, then check the decimal point: 2.5 × 4 = 10.

items.q: What is the volume of this rectangular prism?
items.e: V = 1.5 × 2 × 3 = 3 × 3 = 9 m³. Multiply decimals the same way, then check the decimal point: 1.5 × 2 = 3.

items.q: A rectangular prism has a volume of 240 cm³. It is 10 cm long and 4 cm wide. How high is it?
A rectangular prism has a volume of 360 cm³. It is 9 cm long and 8 cm high. How wide is it?
A rectangular prism has a volume of 500 cm³. It is 10 cm long and 10 cm wide. How high is it?
Which box has a volume of 24 cm³?
items.e: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cm³. 10 + 8 + 6 is 24, but its volume is 10 × 8 × 6 = 480 cm³. 8 × 3 = 24 forgets the third edge: 8 × 3 × 3 = 72 cm³.

items.q: A box is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high. Its length doubles to 10 cm and the other edges stay the same. What is the new volume?
items.e: Old volume: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 cm³. New volume: 10 × 4 × 3 = 120 cm³. Doubling one edge doubles the volume. 480 cm³ would need all three edges doubled.

items.q: How many millilitres are in 3 L?
How many millilitres are in 2.5 L?
items.e: 1 L = 1000 mL, so multiply by 1000: 2.5 × 1000 = 2500 mL. 2.5 L is not 2 L 5 mL.

items.q: How many millilitres are in 1.2 L?
items.e: 1 L = 1000 mL, so multiply by 1000: 1.2 × 1000 = 1200 mL. 1.2 L is not 1 L 2 mL.

items.q: How many millilitres are in 0.75 L?
How many litres are in 4000 mL?
items.e: 1000 mL = 1 L, so divide by 1000: 4000 ÷ 1000 = 4 L. (Dividing by 100 gives 40, which is 10 times too big.)

items.q: How many litres are in 1500 mL?
items.e: 1000 mL = 1 L, so divide by 1000: 1500 ÷ 1000 = 1.5 L. (Dividing by 100 gives 15, which is 10 times too big.)

items.q: How many litres are in 2300 mL?
items.e: 1000 mL = 1 L, so divide by 1000: 2300 ÷ 1000 = 2.3 L. (Dividing by 100 gives 23, which is 10 times too big.)

items.q: How many litres are in 250 mL?
items.e: 1000 mL = 1 L, so divide by 1000: 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.25 L. (Dividing by 100 gives 2.5, which is 10 times too big.)

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The labels go up by 200 mL, and there are 4 spaces between labels, so each small mark is 200 ÷ 4 = 50 mL. The water is 1 mark above 600 mL: 600 + 50 = 650 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The labels go up by 200 mL, and there are 4 spaces between labels, so each small mark is 200 ÷ 4 = 50 mL. The water is 2 marks above 200 mL: 200 + 100 = 300 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The labels go up by 200 mL, and there are 4 spaces between labels, so each small mark is 200 ÷ 4 = 50 mL. The water is 2 marks above 800 mL: 800 + 100 = 900 mL.

items.q: Which amount is the most?
items.e: Change all of them to millilitres: 1.5 L = 1500 mL and 0.95 L = 950 mL. 1500 > 1200 > 980 > 950, so 1.5 L is the most. A big number in mL can still be less.

items.q: Which amount is the least?
items.e: 0.4 L = 400 mL, 0.5 L = 500 mL and 1.1 L = 1100 mL. So 350 mL is the least, even though 0.4 looks small.

items.q: Which amount is equal to 2.05 L?
items.e: 2.05 × 1000 = 2050 mL. The 0 in the tenths place holds the place: 2.05 L is 2 L and 50 mL.

items.q: About how much does a teaspoon hold?
items.e: A teaspoon holds a tiny amount: about 5 mL. 500 mL is a big water bottle, and 5 L is a big jug.

items.q: About how much water does a full bathtub hold?
items.e: A bathtub holds a lot: about 150 L. 15 L would fill only about one bucket and a half.

items.q: About how much does a juice box hold?
items.e: A juice box is small enough for a lunch bag: about 200 mL. 2 L is a big bottle of juice.

items.q: Ava drinks 750 mL of water in the morning and 1.5 L in the afternoon. How much does she drink in all?
items.e: Use the same unit first: 1.5 L = 1500 mL. 750 + 1500 = 2250 mL (2.25 L). 751.5 adds 750 and 1.5 without changing the units.

items.q: How many 250 mL glasses can you fill from a full 2 L jug?
items.e: 2 L = 2000 mL. 2000 ÷ 250 = 8 glasses. (4 glasses is only 1 L, and 80 uses 2 L = 20 000 mL.)

items.q: A 2 L bottle of water is full. Mateo pours out 650 mL. How much is left?
items.e: 2 L = 2000 mL. 2000 − 650 = 1350 mL. 648 takes 2 away from 650 without changing the units, and 2650 adds instead of subtracting.

items.q: A container has a volume of 1 cm³. How much water can it hold?
items.e: 1 cm³ holds exactly 1 mL. That is the key link between volume and capacity.

items.q: A cube-shaped container is 10 cm long, 10 cm wide and 10 cm high inside. How much water does it hold?
items.e: V = 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cm³ = 1000 mL = 1 L. (100 is only the base, and 30 adds the edges.)

items.q: A small box is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 10 cm high inside. How many millilitres of water can it hold?
items.e: V = 5 × 4 × 10 = 200 cm³, and 1 cm³ holds 1 mL, so it holds 200 mL.

items.q: A small box is 8 cm long, 5 cm wide and 6 cm high inside. How many millilitres of water can it hold?
items.e: V = 8 × 5 × 6 = 240 cm³, and 1 cm³ holds 1 mL, so it holds 240 mL.

items.q: A small box is 12 cm long, 5 cm wide and 5 cm high inside. How many millilitres of water can it hold?
items.e: V = 12 × 5 × 5 = 300 cm³, and 1 cm³ holds 1 mL, so it holds 300 mL.

items.q: A small box is 10 cm long, 10 cm wide and 4 cm high inside. How many millilitres of water can it hold?
items.e: V = 10 × 10 × 4 = 400 cm³, and 1 cm³ holds 1 mL, so it holds 400 mL.

items.q: A small box is 9 cm long, 6 cm wide and 5 cm high inside. How many millilitres of water can it hold?
items.e: V = 9 × 6 × 5 = 270 cm³, and 1 cm³ holds 1 mL, so it holds 270 mL.

items.q: This container is full of water. How many litres does it hold?
This container is full of water. How many litres does it hold?
This container is full of water. How many litres does it hold?
A container has a volume of 3000 cm³. How many litres can it hold?
items.e: 3000 cm³ = 3000 mL. Divide by 1000 to get litres: 3 L.

items.q: A container has a volume of 1500 cm³. How many litres can it hold?
items.e: 1500 cm³ = 1500 mL. Divide by 1000 to get litres: 1.5 L.

items.q: A container has a volume of 750 cm³. How many litres can it hold?
items.e: 750 cm³ = 750 mL. Divide by 1000 to get litres: 0.75 L.

items.q: A measuring jug has 300 mL of water. Kai drops a rock into it, and the water rises to 340 mL. What is the volume of the rock?
items.e: The rock pushes the water up by the space it takes. 340 − 300 = 40 mL, and 1 mL = 1 cm³, so the rock is 40 cm³.

items.q: A measuring jug has 500 mL of water. Zara drops a rock into it, and the water rises to 575 mL. What is the volume of the rock?
items.e: The rock pushes the water up by the space it takes. 575 − 500 = 75 mL, and 1 mL = 1 cm³, so the rock is 75 cm³.

items.q: A measuring jug has 1.2 L of water. Lucas drops a small rock into it, and the water rises to 1.45 L. What is the volume of the rock?
items.e: The rock pushes the water up by the space it takes. First change litres to millilitres: 1.2 L = 1200 mL and 1.45 L = 1450 mL. 1450 − 1200 = 250 mL, and 1 mL = 1 cm³, so the rock is 250 cm³.

items.q: A cube-shaped tank is 1 m long, 1 m wide and 1 m high inside. How many litres does it hold?
Which box holds exactly 1 L?
items.e: 1 L = 1000 mL = 1000 cm³. 20 × 5 × 10 = 1000 cm³. The others hold 500 mL, 100 mL and 10 L. A box does not need to be a 10 cm cube to hold 1 L.

items.q: A box has a base 10 cm long and 10 cm wide. It holds 500 mL when full. How high is it?
items.e: 500 mL = 500 cm³. Base: 10 × 10 = 100 cm². Height = 500 ÷ 100 = 5 cm. 50 cm divides by only one edge.

items.q: A milk carton holds 1 L. Its base is 10 cm long and 5 cm wide. How high is the milk when the carton is full?
items.e: 1 L = 1000 cm³. Base: 10 × 5 = 50 cm². Height = 1000 ÷ 50 = 20 cm. 100 and 200 divide by only one edge.

sets.title: Word problems: fish tanks and boxes

items.q: A juice box is 6 cm long, 4 cm wide and 10 cm high. How much juice can it hold?
items.e: V = 6 × 4 × 10 = 240 cm³. 1 cm³ = 1 mL, so it holds 240 mL. (2.4 L would be 2400 mL.)

items.q: A shoebox is 30 cm long, 20 cm wide and 12 cm high. What is its volume?
items.e: V = 30 × 20 × 12 = 600 × 12 = 7200 cm³. 600 is only the base, and volume is in cm³, not cm².

items.q: Liam’s fish tank is 60 cm long, 30 cm wide and 40 cm high. How many litres does it hold when full?
Liam fills the same fish tank (60 cm long, 30 cm wide, 40 cm high) only up to 35 cm. How much water is in it?
items.e: Use the height of the water, not the tank: 60 × 30 × 35 = 1800 × 35 = 63 000 cm³ = 63 L. 9 L is the empty space at the top.

items.q: Ji-woo’s fish tank is 50 cm long, 25 cm wide and 30 cm high. How many litres does it hold when full?
A cooler for a class field trip is 40 cm long, 30 cm wide and 25 cm deep inside. How many litres does it hold?
Arjun’s lunch container is 15 cm long, 10 cm wide and 6 cm high. Will 1 L of soup fit in it?
items.e: V = 15 × 10 × 6 = 900 cm³ = 900 mL. 1 L = 1000 mL, so no: 100 mL of soup would not fit.

items.q: Box A is 8 cm × 5 cm × 4 cm. Box B is 6 cm × 6 cm × 5 cm. Which box has the greater volume, and by how much?
items.e: A: 8 × 5 × 4 = 160 cm³. B: 6 × 6 × 5 = 180 cm³. 180 − 160 = 20, so B is greater by 20 cm³. Adding the edges gives 17 for both boxes, which is why “the same” is a trap.

items.q: A tissue box is a cube with edges 12 cm long. What is its volume?
items.e: V = 12 × 12 × 12 = 144 × 12 = 1728 cm³. 144 is only one face, and 36 adds the edges.

items.q: Olivia’s water bottle holds 750 mL. On a hike up Grouse Mountain, she drinks 3 full bottles. How many litres does she drink?
items.e: 3 × 750 = 2250 mL. Divide by 1000: 2.25 L. (2250 L forgets to change mL to L.)

items.q: A school in Surrey builds a sandbox 3 m long and 2 m wide. The sand is 0.5 m deep. How much sand is that?
items.e: V = 3 × 2 × 0.5 = 6 × 0.5 = 3 m³. (6 is only the area of the base, and 5.5 adds the edges.)

items.q: A rectangular rain barrel in Vancouver is 50 cm long, 40 cm wide and 80 cm high. How many litres of rain can it hold?
How many 2 cm cubes fit in a box that is 10 cm long, 6 cm wide and 4 cm high?
items.e: Along the length: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cubes. Across: 6 ÷ 2 = 3. Up: 4 ÷ 2 = 2. 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 cubes. 240 counts 1 cm cubes, and 120 divides by 2 only once.

items.q: A rectangular tank at a salmon hatchery on Vancouver Island is 4 m long and 2 m wide. The water is 1 m deep. How many litres of water are in the tank?
A water tank in an Okanagan orchard is 2 m long, 1.5 m wide and 1 m high. How many litres does it hold?
Hana builds a cedar planter box that is 120 cm long, 40 cm wide and 30 cm deep inside. Soil comes in 50 L bags. How many bags does she need to fill the box?
items.e: V = 120 × 40 × 30 = 144 000 cm³ = 144 L. 144 ÷ 50 = 2.88, so 2 bags are not enough. She needs 3 bags.

items.q: A hose fills Liam’s 72 L fish tank at 4 L per minute. How many minutes does it take to fill the tank?
items.e: 72 ÷ 4 = 18 minutes. Check: 18 × 4 = 72 L. (288 multiplies, and 68 subtracts.)

items.q: An aquarium has a base 50 cm long and 25 cm wide. Ethan pours in 25 L of water. How deep is the water?
items.e: 25 L = 25 000 cm³. Base: 50 × 25 = 1250 cm². Depth = 25 000 ÷ 1250 = 20 cm. 500 divides by the length only.

items.q: A storage bin holds 60 L. Its inside base is 50 cm long and 40 cm wide. How high is the inside of the bin?
items.e: 60 L = 60 000 cm³. Base: 50 × 40 = 2000 cm². Height = 60 000 ÷ 2000 = 30 cm. 1200 divides by the length only.

items.q: Emma has an empty cube-shaped container with 20 cm edges. She pours in 4 L of water. How deep is the water?
items.e: 4 L = 4000 cm³. Base: 20 × 20 = 400 cm². Depth = 4000 ÷ 400 = 10 cm, so the container is half full. 200 cm divides by one edge only.
